## claude.ai HyperFrames by HeyGen

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.
- This MCP → hosted HeyGen project with a `project_id`, a live canvas at
  `app.heygen.com/projects/{id}`, and the cloud render queue.

Route by what the user actually wants:
- "Make a local HTML composition / something I can edit" → use a local skill.
- "Make a HeyGen project I can share / render in the cloud / open in the app"
  → use this MCP, even from a CLI agent.

## What it does

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects… [truncated]

# RTP_Constraints_Course

A **teaching workspace**, not a code project. It runs on Matt Pocock's `teach` skill
(mattpocock-skills 1.2.3).

**Learner:** Joe Smith, assistant athletic trainer, Baylor Athletics.
**Sponsor:** Eric Rash.
**Topic:** ecological dynamics and the constraints-led approach (CLA) applied to the last
phase of return to performance in American football.

## How to work here

Type `/teach` in this directory. Do not hand-roll lessons — the skill owns the workflow.
`teach` and `ask-matt` are `disable-model-invocation: true`, so **a human must type the
slash command**; the agent cannot invoke them.

Read before doing anything: `MISSION.md`, then `NOTES.md` (open questions and framing
wrinkles), then `RESOURCES.md`.

## Layout

| Path | What it is |
|---|---|
| `MISSION.md` | Why Joe is learning this. Grounds every teaching decision. |
| `INTERVIEW.md` | **Mission interview to run with Joe. Do this before lesson 0001.** 45 min; Parts 1 and 2 are the ones that matter. Run 2026-09-03. |
| `interviews/` | Transcripts of interviews actually run, plus a key-answers digest. Joe's mission interview lives here. **Names athletes and their injuries — never commit, never paste into an artifact or an external service.** |
| `RESOURCES.md` | Curated trusted sources. Most are already in Eric's SecondBrain library. |
| `NOTES.md` | Open questions, preferences, working notes. |
| `assets/` | Reusable lesson components. `course.css` is shared by every lesson. |
| `lessons/` | `NNNN-slug.html` — the unit of teaching. None written yet. |
| `reference/` | `*.html` cheat sheets. The compressed residue of lessons. |
| `sources/` | Full-text books and long PDFs obtained legitimately. Author-supplied — **never redistribute, never commit.** |
| `docs/handoffs/` | Durable cross-session handoffs. Newest first. |
| `learning-records/` | `NNNN-slug.md` ADR-style records. Created lazily at the first record. |

## Rules specific to this workspace

- **Ground in `RESOURCES.md`, never in parametric knowledge.** This field has a lot of
  confident bad writing in it. Cite everything.
- **Football examples only.** Generic team-sport examples will not land with position coaches.
- **Every lesson ends in something Joe could do at practice tomorrow.**

- **Phase 2 is a drill-design tool.** Do not start it until the lessons have specified it.
  Route: `/grill-with-docs` → `/prototype` → `/implement`. Local-only per Baylor IT.

## Source library

Papers referenced as `LIB/…` live in `~/SecondBrain/Knowledge/library/research-papers/`.
Search with `memsearch search "<query>" --top-k 5`. Zotero MCP was down on 2026-09-01.

The user has asked you to teach them something. This is a stateful request - they intend to learn the topic over multiple sessions.

## Teaching Workspace

Treat the current directory as a teaching workspace. The state of their learning is captured in this directory in several files:

- `MISSION.md`: A document capturing the _reason_ the user is interested in the topic. This should be used to ground all teaching. Use the format in [MISSION-FORMAT.md](./MISSION-FORMAT.md).
- `./reference/*.html`: A directory of reference materials. These are the compressed learnings from the lessons - cheat sheets, reference algorithms, syntax, yoga poses, glossaries. They are the raw units of learning. They should be beautiful documents which print out well, and are designed for quick reference.
- `RESOURCES.md`: A list of resources which can be explored to ground your teaching in contextual knowledge, or to acquire knowledge and wisdom. Use the format in [RESOURCES-FORMAT.md](./RESOURCES-FORMAT.md).
- `./learning-records/*.md`: A directory of learning records, which capture what the user has learned. These are loosely equivalent to architectural decision records in software development - they capture non-obvious lessons and key insights that may need to be revised later, or drive future sessions. These should be used to calculate the zone of proximal development. They are titled `0001-<dash-case-name>.md`, where the number increments each time. Use the format in [LEARNING-RECORD-FORMAT.md](./LEARNING-RECORD-FORMAT.md).
- `./lessons/*.html`: A directory of lessons. A **lesson** is a single, self-contained HTML output that teaches one tightly-scoped thing tied to the mission. This is the primary unit of teaching in this workspace.
- `./assets/*`: Reusable **components** shared across lessons. See [Assets](#assets).
- `NOTES.md`: A scratchpad for you to jot down user preferences, or working notes.

## Philosophy

To learn at a deep level, the user needs three things:

- **Knowledge**, captured from high-quality, high-trust resources
- **Skills**, acquired through highly-relevant interactive lessons devised by you, based on the knowledge
- **Wisdom**, which comes from interacting with other learners and practitioners

Before the `RESOURCES.md` is well-populated, your focus should be to find high-quality resources which will help the user acquire knowledge. Never trust your parametric knowledge.

Some topics may require more skills than knowledge. Learning more about theoretical physics might be more knowledge-based. For yoga, more skills-based.

### Fluency vs Storage Strength

You should be careful to split between two types of learning:

- **Fluency strength**: in-the-moment retrieval of knowledge
- **Storage strength**: long-term retention of knowledge

Fluency can give the user an illusory sense of mastery, but storage strength is the real goal. Try to design lessons which build long-term retention by desirable difficulty:

- Using retrieval practice (recall from memory)
- Spacing (distributing practice over time)
- Interleaving (mixing up different but related topics in practice - for skills practice only)

## Lessons

A lesson is the main thing you produce — the unit in which knowledge and skills reach the user. Each lesson is one self-contained HTML file, saved to `./lessons/` and titled `0001-<dash-case-name>.html` where the number increments each time.

A lesson should be **beautiful** — clean, readable typography and layout — since the user will return to these later to review. Think Tufte.

The lesson should be short, and completable very quickly. Learners' working memory is very small, and we need to stay within it. But each lesson should give the user a single tangible win that they can build on. It should be directly tied to the mission, and should be in the user's zone of proximal development.

If possible, open the lesson file for the user by running a CLI command.

Each lesson should link via HTML anchors to other lessons and reference documents.

Each lesson should recommend a primary source for the user to read or watch. This should be the most high-quality, high-trust resource you found on the topic.

Each lesson should contain a reminder to ask followup questions to the agent. The agent is their teacher, and can assist with anything that's unclear.

## Assets

Lessons are built from reusable **components**, stored in `./assets/`: stylesheets, quiz widgets, simulators, diagram helpers — anything a second lesson could reuse.

Reuse is the default, not the exception. Before authoring a lesson, read `./assets/` and build from the components already there. When a lesson needs something new and reusable, write it as a component in `./assets/` and link to it — never inline code a future lesson would duplicate.

A shared stylesheet is the first component every workspace earns: every lesson links it, so the lessons look like one consistent course rather than a pile of one-offs. As the workspace grows, so should the component library.

## The Mission

Every lesson should be tied into the mission - the reason that the user is interested in learning about the topic.

If the user is unclear about the mission, or the `MISSION.md` is not populated, your first job should be to question the user on why they want to learn this.

Failing to understand the mission will mean knowledge acquisition is not grounded in real-world goals. Lessons will feel too abstract. You will have no way of judging what the user should do next.

Missions may change as the user develops more skills and knowledge. This is normal - make sure to update the `MISSION.md` and add a learning record to capture the change. Confirm with the user before changing the mission.

## Zone Of Proximal Development

Each lesson, the user should always feel as if they are being challenged 'just enough'.

The user may specify an exact thing they want to learn. If they don't, figure out their zone of proximal development by:

- Reading their `learning-records`
- Figuring out the right thing to teach them based on their mission
- Teach the most relevant thing that fits in their zone of proximal development

## Knowledge

Lessons should be designed around a skill the user is going to learn. The knowledge in the lesson should be only what's required to acquire that skill. You teach the knowledge first, then get the user to practice the skills via an interactive feedback loop.

Knowledge should first be gathered from trusted resources. Use `RESOURCES.md` to keep track of them. Lessons should be littered with citations - links to external resources to back up any claim made. This increases the trustworthiness of the lesson.

For acquiring knowledge, difficulty is the enemy. It eats working memory you need for understanding.

## Skills

If knowledge is all about acquisition, skills are about durability and flexibility. Make the knowledge stick.

For skill acquisition, difficulty is the tool. Effortful retrieval is what builds storage strength. Skills should be taught through interactive lessons. There are several tools at your disposal:

- Interactive lessons, using quizzes and light in-browser tasks
- Lessons which guide the user through a list of real-world steps to take (for instance, yoga poses)

Each of these should be based on a **feedback loop**, where the user receives feedback on their performance. This feedback loop should be as tight as possible, giving feedback immediately - and ideally automatically.

For quizzes, each answer should be exactly the same number of words (and characters, if possible). Don't give the user any clues about the answer through formatting.

## Acquiring Wisdom

Wisdom comes from true real-world interaction - testing your skills outside the learning environment.

When the user asks a question that appears to require wisdom, your default posture should be to attempt to answer - but to ultimately delegate to a **community**.

A community is a place (online or offline) where the user can test their skills in the real world. This might be a forum, a subreddit, a real-world class (budget permitting) or a local interest group.

You should attempt to find high-reputation communities the user can join. If the user expresses a preference that they don't want to join a community, respect it.

## Reference Documents

While creating lessons, you should also create reference documents. Lessons can reference these documents - they are useful for tracking raw units of knowledge useful across lessons.

Lessons will rarely be revisited later - reference documents will be. They should be the compressed essence of the lesson, in a format designed for quick reference.

Some learning topics lend themselves to reference:

- Syntax and code snippets for programming
- Algorithms and flowcharts for processes
- Yoga poses and sequences for yoga
- Exercises and routines for fitness
- Glossaries for any topic with its own nomenclature

Glossaries, in particular, are an essential reference. Once one is created, it should be adhered to in every lesson.

## `NOTES.md`

The user will sometimes express preferences of how they want to be taught, or things you should keep in mind. This is the place to record those preferences, so you can refer back to them when designing lessons or working with the user.

# Mission: Constraints-Led Return to Performance (American Football)

> **Confirmed with Joe on 2026-09-03**, in a 47.8-minute mission interview run from
> `INTERVIEW.md`. Every claim below traces to something Joe said. Source and timestamps:
> `interviews/2026-09-03-joe-smith-mission-interview.md`.
> Quoted lines are Joe's own words.

## Why

Joe Smith (assistant athletic trainer, Baylor Athletics) wants to own return to
performance at Baylor football. In his words: *"I want to be known as the guy in this
room that does return to performance… and that I make our football team better by the
return to performance that the guys complete."*

He draws a hard line between **return to play** and **return to performance**. Return to
play is when drills begin to look and feel like football. Return to performance is when
you are chasing back the level the player actually held before. His test for it: *"I
could go out there and play football. I would not be expected to perform at the same
level that our guys are."* He wants that distinction written into the Baylor framework,
and says the sheet already in use has room for it.

What he is not asking for is a way to fill the post-clearance gap. **He explicitly
rejected that boundary.** The work starts at the back end of rehab, before clearance, and
it also covers acute cases — players who are never held out at all, which is most of what
he does day to day.

The method he already runs is a needs assessment, then a **reverse calendar** worked
backwards from the target event, then density and intensity set per day. That method is
sound and stays. What it lacks is a defensible account of *why* a given exposure is the
right one — and that is the gap this course fills.

The sharpest thing Joe said about his own weakness: *"I'm least confident in the ability
to rationalize a very subjective process to objectively oriented people."*

**That sentence is the mission.** Joe does not need convincing that this work matters. He
needs language, structure and evidence that survive a hostile question from someone who
was not there.

## Success looks like

- Joe can explain to a skeptical position coach why a pre-planned cone drill is not evidence of readiness.
- **Joe can defend a subjective judgement to an objective audience** — naming the information the athlete had to use, the problem the exposure posed, and why the result counts as evidence. This is the one that matters most to him.
- Joe can name the three constraint classes — performer, task, environment — and deliberately manipulate each to raise or lower a drill's demand.
- **Joe can say why his non-reactive drills flatter an athlete**, and design the reactive exposure that finds what they hide. He has already seen this happen with a returning offensive lineman; he does not yet have the vocabulary for it.
- Joe can state, for a given position and injury, what perceptual information that job actually requires, and judge whether a drill samples it (representative design).
- Joe can build a progression from controlled to chaotic and say out loud where a given athlete sits on it, and why.
- **Joe can name when he is not the right constraint.** He cannot load a lineman at his own size, and had to bring in a position coach and real bodies to finish that case. He should be able to say when a person, not a drill, is the missing piece.
- Joe can apply all of the above in the **acute** case, not only after a long rehab.
- Joe can spec a session in under 10 minutes using the drill-design tool built at the end of this course.

## Constraints

- **Joe is a clinician, not a researcher.** Lessons must be short, practical, and free of statistics-heavy reading.
- **Time: about 4 hours a week in season, spread across 7 days; 3–4 hours across 5 days off season.** Confirmed by Joe.
- **He learns badly in fragments.** *"I want to take notes, I want to like reread… really think about something to truly understand it."* A lesson billed at 20 minutes will cost him 30–35. **Size lessons for the way he actually works, not for the clock.**
- **Feedback must coach, not just correct.** *"I love to know when I'm wrong, and I'd love to be coached… if you're gonna tell me I'm wrong, I want to know how to fix it."* Never flag an error without a route out of it.
- **Starting knowledge is zero.** Ecological dynamics: he has heard the term only from Eric. CLA: heard of it, never implemented it, holds no opinion. Assume nothing.
- **Joe does not own medical clearance.** The method has to slot into the existing physician/ATC chain, not replace it. Jacob (director of rehab) and Tim (head athletic trainer) are the gatekeepers.
- **It must survive people who were not in the room.** Expect two objections: that a dedicated person is a poor use of resources because every athletic trainer should run return-to-play progressions, and that this should be a weight-room collaboration instead. Joe needs an answer to both.
- **American football only.** Position-specific, contact sport, high chaos. Every position, quarterback to kicker.
- **Delivery:** at his laptop, in the office. All standard equipment available. GPS, force plates and force frame are available and are not a limiter. He is willing to film sessions.
- **Tool must run locally** — no cloud services or servers without Baylor IT approval.

## Out of scope

## The drill-design tool — Joe's specification

Recorded from the interview so it is not lost. **Do not build it yet; the lessons specify
it.** Full detail with timestamps in the interview digest.

**Inputs:** injury type, split structural/mechanical (watch shifting, popping, clicking)
versus muscle belly (watch pain, tension, tightness) · previous exposure and the response
to it, his read and the athlete's · the needs assessment · the target event, including
sub-events on a long rehab.

checklist of qualities covered — reactive and non-reactive, explosive and non-explosive,
joint angles, plus an aerobic/anaerobic layer · if-yes/if-no branches, so there is a plan
B when the athlete presents differently than expected.

**It does not go in the EMR.** It is an aid; Joe writes his note afterwards anyway.

## What would make Joe walk

Not the learning — he said nothing would take him away from the work itself. What would
take him away from doing it **here** is the value being recognised by the people close to
it in football, and not matched by support from outside that circle.

**Implication for this course:** the artefacts have to travel. Something Joe can hand to
someone who was never at the practice is not a nice-to-have.

**Do not re-derive this.** Rob Gray states an operational rule in [the 3 Questions video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Z0pLFDG-I78) (47 min, transcribed 2026-09-02; full notes in `RESOURCES.md`):

- **Success rate is the trigger — not reps, not minutes, not the clinician's eye.**
- **Above ~75% success -> add a constraint or complexity. Below ~70% -> reduce variability. Inside 70-75% -> leave it alone.**
- Loop: choose the **invariant** (never the technique) -> add one constraint -> **watch 5-6+ trials** -> changing in the right direction? leave it -> stabilised or stuck? manipulate it -> no effect at all? bin it and design another.
- **Same drill, opposite directions for different athletes:** the one succeeding gets more variability, the one failing gets less. **A progression/regression rule built purely from drill design — the proof that the design layer and the RTP dosing layer are one skill.**

**Input model (added 2026-09-02 from the [Gray-Sarama interview](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iTXMVsSu1Q0)):
the tool must ask for a RATE LIMITER, not a vague goal.** "Improve his cutting" is useless. Sarama's
worked example: not "he's bad at rebounding" but (a) not attuning to ball flight, ~2 s late to look,
and (b) positioning under the basket where no rebound exists. **The tool should reject vague input
and push for that level of specificity** — it is what makes a constraint choosable at all. Pair it
with a one-page sheet: every athlete's name, their rate limiters, and one person whose job in the
session is individualising constraints.

the resolution genuinely open. **The cleanest way to give a returning athlete repeated exposure to one
specific problem without deleting the perception** — and the answer to the medical-staff safety objection.

**70-75%** is the sweet spot. Sarama, independently and without reference to Gray, treats **~60%** as

ceiling (~80% = make it harder), and differ on the target by 10-15 points.** **Ship it as a
user-settable range labelled with both attributions, never as one validated-looking number.**

# Mission: Constraints-Led Return to Performance (American Football)

> **Confirmed with Joe on 2026-09-03**, in a 47.8-minute mission interview run from
> `INTERVIEW.md`. Every claim below traces to something Joe said. Source and timestamps:
> `interviews/2026-09-03-joe-smith-mission-interview.md`.
> Quoted lines are Joe's own words.

## Why

Joe Smith (assistant athletic trainer, Baylor Athletics) wants to own return to
performance at Baylor football. In his words: *"I want to be known as the guy in this
room that does return to performance… and that I make our football team better by the
return to performance that the guys complete."*

He draws a hard line between **return to play** and **return to performance**. Return to
play is when drills begin to look and feel like football. Return to performance is when
you are chasing back the level the player actually held before. His test for it: *"I
could go out there and play football. I would not be expected to perform at the same
level that our guys are."* He wants that distinction written into the Baylor framework,
and says the sheet already in use has room for it.

What he is not asking for is a way to fill the post-clearance gap. **He explicitly
rejected that boundary.** The work starts at the back end of rehab, before clearance, and
it also covers acute cases — players who are never held out at all, which is most of what
he does day to day.

The method he already runs is a needs assessment, then a **reverse calendar** worked
backwards from the target event, then density and intensity set per day. That method is
sound and stays. What it lacks is a defensible account of *why* a given exposure is the
right one — and that is the gap this course fills.

The sharpest thing Joe said about his own weakness: *"I'm least confident in the ability
to rationalize a very subjective process to objectively oriented people."*

**That sentence is the mission.** Joe does not need convincing that this work matters. He
needs language, structure and evidence that survive a hostile question from someone who
was not there.

## Success looks like

- Joe can explain to a skeptical position coach why a pre-planned cone drill is not evidence of readiness.
- **Joe can defend a subjective judgement to an objective audience** — naming the information the athlete had to use, the problem the exposure posed, and why the result counts as evidence. This is the one that matters most to him.
- Joe can name the three constraint classes — performer, task, environment — and deliberately manipulate each to raise or lower a drill's demand.
- **Joe can say why his non-reactive drills flatter an athlete**, and design the reactive exposure that finds what they hide. He has already seen this happen with a returning offensive lineman; he does not yet have the vocabulary for it.
- Joe can state, for a given position and injury, what perceptual information that job actually requires, and judge whether a drill samples it (representative design).
- Joe can build a progression from controlled to chaotic and say out loud where a given athlete sits on it, and why.
- **Joe can name when he is not the right constraint.** He cannot load a lineman at his own size, and had to bring in a position coach and real bodies to finish that case. He should be able to say when a person, not a drill, is the missing piece.
- Joe can apply all of the above in the **acute** case, not only after a long rehab.
- Joe can spec a session in under 10 minutes using the drill-design tool built at the end of this course.

## Constraints

- **Joe is a clinician, not a researcher.** Lessons must be short, practical, and free of statistics-heavy reading.
- **Time: about 4 hours a week in season, spread across 7 days; 3–4 hours across 5 days off season.** Confirmed by Joe.
- **He learns badly in fragments.** *"I want to take notes, I want to like reread… really think about something to truly understand it."* A lesson billed at 20 minutes will cost him 30–35. **Size lessons for the way he actually works, not for the clock.**
- **Feedback must coach, not just correct.** *"I love to know when I'm wrong, and I'd love to be coached… if you're gonna tell me I'm wrong, I want to know how to fix it."* Never flag an error without a route out of it.
- **Starting knowledge is zero.** Ecological dynamics: he has heard the term only from Eric. CLA: heard of it, never implemented it, holds no opinion. Assume nothing.
- **Joe does not own medical clearance.** The method has to slot into the existing physician/ATC chain, not replace it. Jacob (director of rehab) and Tim (head athletic trainer) are the gatekeepers.
- **It must survive people who were not in the room.** Expect two objections: that a dedicated person is a poor use of resources because every athletic trainer should run return-to-play progressions, and that this should be a weight-room collaboration instead. Joe needs an answer to both.
- **American football only.** Position-specific, contact sport, high chaos. Every position, quarterback to kicker.
- **Delivery:** at his laptop, in the office. All standard equipment available. GPS, force plates and force frame are available and are not a limiter. He is willing to film sessions.
- **Tool must run locally** — no cloud services or servers without Baylor IT approval.
- Eric Rash commissions and steers this; Joe is the learner. **Confirmed 2026-09-03** — Joe asked whether Eric intends to do this for other young professionals, and is treating it as a career move rather than a favour.

## Out of scope

- Early-stage rehabilitation, tissue healing timelines, and the criteria for medical clearance itself. **The course does cover the back end of rehab before clearance — it just does not decide clearance.**
- Motor-learning theory disputes (schema theory vs. ecological) beyond the minimum needed to defend a drill.
- Sports other than American football.
- Building a full athlete-management system. The deliverable is one focused drill-design tool.
- Cases with no performance level to rebuild. Joe's own example is rhabdomyolysis: an evaluation question, not a return-to-performance one.

## The drill-design tool — Joe's specification

Recorded from the interview so it is not lost. **Do not build it yet; the lessons specify
it.** Full detail with timestamps in the interview digest.

**Inputs:** injury type, split structural/mechanical (watch shifting, popping, clicking)
versus muscle belly (watch pain, tension, tightness) · previous exposure and the response
to it, his read and the athlete's · the needs assessment · the target event, including
sub-events on a long rehab.

**Outputs:** a reverse calendar of the progression — **explicitly not "gradual"**, because
Joe wants spikes, hills and valleys and treats the response to a spike as information ·
research-backed numbers where they exist, particularly return-to-run and high-speed
running for hamstrings · density and intensity blocks that undulate with the team week
(Tue/Wed high, Thu low, Fri/Sat up), which he admits he currently does sporadically · a
checklist of qualities covered — reactive and non-reactive, explosive and non-explosive,
joint angles, plus an aerobic/anaerobic layer · if-yes/if-no branches, so there is a plan
B when the athlete presents differently than expected.

**It does not go in the EMR.** It is an aid; Joe writes his note afterwards anyway.

## What would make Joe walk

Not the learning — he said nothing would take him away from the work itself. What would
take him away from doing it **here** is the value being recognised by the people close to
it in football, and not matched by support from outside that circle.

**Implication for this course:** the artefacts have to travel. Something Joe can hand to
someone who was never at the practice is not a nice-to-have.

# Working Notes

## Open questions for Eric (asked 2026-09-01, not yet answered)

**These are now questions 15 and 23 in `INTERVIEW.md` (written 2026-09-02). Ask Joe, not Eric —

## Teaching approach

**FOUR lesson-0001 candidates are listed below, in the order the research turned them up. They are
candidates, not a ranking — none has been chosen. The `/teach` session picks one and records the
choice as a learning record. Ignore the word "strongest" in the older bullets; it accumulated.**

- The strongest hook available: **"agility and change-of-direction speed are independent
  skills"** (Young 2015, in the library). **VERIFY THE CITATION FIRST (flagged 2026-09-02):**

  of the IUSCA"** (`R656I7IY`) has been sitting in `RESOURCES.md` all along, in the football-demands

  specifically about **invasion sports** — i.e. football. **Check which paper actually makes the
  agility-vs-COD claim, then cite the stronger one.** A hook that opens lesson 0001 must not rest on

  one citation. Strong candidate for lesson 0001.
- **Rival hook, found 2026-09-02 — arguably stronger because it indicts a habit Joe already has:**

  a task down to no defender. **ATTRIBUTION WARNING: this sentence is not a quotation and is not
  Sarama's.** The Transforming Basketball source (written by George Vaz) says only *reduce
  defensive pressure rather than remove the defender*, as a coaching point about beginners, with
  no mention of injury. **The extension to return-to-play is ours.** Teach it, but source it to
  Parry (2025) on opposed vs unopposed practice (`CA2CRR6Z`) — never to Sarama. **Young 2015 reframes cone drills; this reframes every
  return-to-play progression Joe has ever run. Decide between them at lesson 0001.**
- **Strongest through-line found so far (2026-09-02), and a better spine than either single hook:
  the attentional-focus chain.** Gray (2015) shows injury *causes* an internal focus on the injured
  part, which measurably degrades performance → the Emergence blog adds that anxiety shrinks
  perceived affordances → Singh/Gokeler/Benjaminse (`EYKZD68B`, owned) gives the ACL clinical
  evidence → the coaching fix is to cue the effect, not the body part. **Cause → mechanism →
  clinical evidence → what to say at practice tomorrow.** It explains the athlete who passes every
  physical test and still does not play like himself, and it frames that as a *performance* problem,
  which is Joe's to solve rather than the physician's. **Only Gray (2015) has to be acquired.**
  Full citation chain in `RESOURCES.md`, "Rob Gray" section. **Kept as one strong lesson, not as the
  course spine — see the drill-design note above.**
- **Best free teaching material found (2026-09-02): Rob Gray's [perceptionaction.com](https://perceptionaction.com/) — eight free infographics.**
  Two matter most. **[Comparative Training Studies](https://perceptionaction.com/comparative/)** puts
  traditional against ecological coaching head to head — **that is the page Joe brings when a physician
  or position coach pushes back**, and he will get pushed back. **[Two Approaches](https://perceptionaction.com/approaches/)**
  lays out information-processing vs ecological side by side, so Joe can argue both. The
  **[terminology video](https://youtu.be/EWh0KAHrgIM)** should feed `GLOSSARY.md`. **Download local
  copies — it is one person's site.**
- **Time-sensitive, needs an Eric decision:** Gray teaches a **$1,995 CLA practice-design certification**,
  8 students, with **video feedback on the learner's own practices**. Its syllabus includes *scaling
  constraints to optimize challenge* — the exact question the phase-2 tool must answer. **Winter and
  Spring 2027 are already full; waitlist only.** If Joe is going, the waitlist is a this-week action.
- **STRONGEST lesson-0001 candidate as of 2026-09-02 — beats both hooks above.** Rob Gray's
  **forearm-flyout / connection-ball example** ([CLA 2024](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gEMSjM1VS3c), ~13 min in).
  A pitcher's arm separates early: it **slows the throw AND strains the UCL** — a performance problem
  and an injury problem that are the same problem. The fix is one task constraint (a ball held under
  the arm) and one instruction (*make it fall out forwards*). **No cue ever names the body part**, and
  the direction the ball falls is **transition feedback** — it tells the athlete whether their *search*
  is heading the right way, not how well they performed. **It is the entire course in a single example,
  it is already injury-relevant, and it needs no translation to make sense to a clinician.**
- **Teach "transition feedback" early — Joe almost certainly does not have this concept.** Not
  knowledge of results, not knowledge of performance: feedback on whether the *search for a new
  solution* is going the right way. Promote it to `GLOSSARY.md` when he uses it correctly.
- **Rule for the tool and for every lesson using Baylor data: biomechanics informs the CONSTRAINT,
  never the CUE.** Gray found insufficient hip-shoulder separation and **never told the athlete** —
  telling him to rotate his hips would drive an internal focus. The measurement is for the designer.
  **This governs how force-plate and GPS data may be used in drill design.**
- **Peer-reviewed lesson found 2026-09-02 — and it targets a clinician's reflex directly.** Goes,
  Machado, Bosco Junior, **Araujo**, Leonardo, Bedo & Scaglia (2025), [doi:10.1177/17479541251348090](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/17479541251348090)
  ([Gray's review](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xu39gkvGuVw)). Three coaches ran the same small-sided
  game under four conditions: no intervention, verbal only, task change only, free. **In two of three
  coaches, verbal intervention changed nothing measurable. Changing the task did.** And the most
  experienced coach's players did best when **left completely alone** — the design was already right.
  **Joe's trained reflex under pressure is to coach harder and talk more. This says redesign the task,
  or say nothing. It is peer-reviewed, which most of this file is not.**
- **The tool must cover the whole cycle, not just step one.** Gray's four steps: **design → put in play
  and adapt → guide → reflect and redesign.** A tool that only proposes an initial drill has done a
  quarter of the job. **Adaptation is where the coaches in that study actually differed.**
- Build toward the tool. Each lesson should surface one input the drill-design tool will
  eventually need (constraint class, demand target, chaos level, position, injury).

## The tool — its core logic is now specified (2026-09-02)

**Do not re-derive this.** Rob Gray states an operational rule in [the 3 Questions video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Z0pLFDG-I78) (47 min, transcribed 2026-09-02; full notes in `RESOURCES.md`):

- **Success rate is the trigger — not reps, not minutes, not the clinician's eye.**
- **Above ~75% success -> add a constraint or complexity. Below ~70% -> reduce variability. Inside 70-75% -> leave it alone.**
- Loop: choose the **invariant** (never the technique) -> add one constraint -> **watch 5-6+ trials** -> changing in the right direction? leave it -> stabilised or stuck? manipulate it -> no effect at all? bin it and design another.
- **Same drill, opposite directions for different athletes:** the one succeeding gets more variability, the one failing gets less. **A progression/regression rule built purely from drill design — the proof that the design layer and the RTP dosing layer are one skill.**

**Input model (added 2026-09-02 from the [Gray-Sarama interview](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iTXMVsSu1Q0)):
the tool must ask for a RATE LIMITER, not a vague goal.** "Improve his cutting" is useless. Sarama's
worked example: not "he's bad at rebounding" but (a) not attuning to ball flight, ~2 s late to look,
and (b) positioning under the basket where no rebound exists. **The tool should reject vague input
and push for that level of specificity** — it is what makes a constraint choosable at all. Pair it
with a one-page sheet: every athlete's name, their rate limiters, and one person whose job in the
session is individualising constraints.

**Also from that interview: "scripted start, live finish."** Script the entry to the situation, leave
the resolution genuinely open. **The cleanest way to give a returning athlete repeated exposure to one
specific problem without deleting the perception** — and the answer to the medical-staff safety objection.

**The success band is a PARAMETER, not a constant — the two best sources disagree.** Gray says
**70-75%** is the sweet spot. Sarama, independently and without reference to Gray, treats **~60%** as
already the right challenge. **They agree on the mechanism (success rate is the trigger) and on the
ceiling (~80% = make it harder), and differ on the target by 10-15 points.** **Ship it as a
user-settable range labelled with both attributions, never as one validated-looking number.**

**Treat 70-75% as an exposed, editable default, not a validated threshold** — it is Gray's heuristic from a podcast, not a study.

## The tool (phase 2 — do not start until lessons land)

A drill-design aid, not a database. Joe enters position, injury, phase, and what he is
trying to expose; it returns constraint manipulations to consider and flags whether the
design is representative. Local only, per the Baylor IT constraint.

# Mission interview — Joe Smith

Source: Fireflies transcript, pulled with `fireflies-pp-cli transcripts get <id> --live`.
Speaker labels come from the Fireflies `speakers` array, which is trustworthy.
The AI summary is **not** used here; its speaker attributions have been wrong before.

---

## Key answers

Every line below is drawn from the turns in this file. Timestamps point to the source turn.
Nothing here comes from the Fireflies AI summary.

### Part 1 gate — does Joe want this niche?

**Yes, clearly.** "I want to be known as the guy in this room that does return to
performance… and that I make our football team better by the return to performance that
the guys complete." (02:28) He hesitated once on owning it alone, then confirmed. (07:21)

Joe also asked, unprompted, whether Eric plans to build this for other young
professionals. (01:36) He is treating this as a career move, not a favour.

### Joe's own definition — return to play vs return to performance

Return to play is when drills start to *look and feel* like football. Return to
performance is when you are chasing performance gains back to the level the player held
before. His test: "I could go out there and play football. I would not be expected to
perform at the same level that our guys are." (03:50) He wants that distinction written
into the Baylor framework, and says the sheet in use has space for it. (13:12)

### Correction to Eric's framing — scope is wider than "cleared but not right"

Joe pushed back on the mission draft. He does **not** want the work bounded to the
post-clearance gap. (12:27)

1. It should start at the **back end of rehab, before clearance.**
2. It must include the **acute phase** — his current case and Trayvon Barnes were never
   held out at all.
3. The framework itself must name the play/performance split.

**`MISSION.md` must be rewritten to match this.** The DRAFT banner comes off with it.

### Where the current system fails — worked example

Brody Wilhelm, tight end, torn ACL. Coasted through fourth-quarter drills limited, did
little in spring, ran all summer, did no football return-to-performance work before camp,
then was dropped straight into training camp. Result: knee symptoms, poor subjective
feel, and a position coach who comments on his performance. (09:30) Joe reads the cause
as time of year plus absent involvement, not the surgery.

### Where the current system already works — worked example

Cooper, target game 5 September. Joe's method, in his words (16:44):

1. **Needs assessment** — what does he need, what will the game demand of him?
2. **Reverse calendar** — start at the event, work backwards, negotiate practice count
   with the player, the coaches and Tim.
3. **Density and intensity per day**, set from the needs assessment — a run-blocking day,
   a pass-blocking day, a reaction day built on real Baylor plays written by Craig Watts.

The finding that matters for the course: **non-reactive drills hid the deficit.** Cooper
was old and sophisticated enough to time them up and looked strong. The reactive pass
drills exposed it — worse performance, more strain reported on the pec. (20:25) Joe also
cannot load a D-lineman properly at his own size, so Coach Watts and D-line bodies had to
be brought in for the last step.

That is a constraints argument Joe already made without the vocabulary for it.

### Prior knowledge — start from zero

- **Ecological dynamics: none.** He has heard the term only from Eric. (14:34)
- **Constraints-led approach: very little.** Heard of it, never implemented it, holds no

=====RES 26-40=====
## Knowledge — Anchor sources (already in the library)

- **Yearby, T., Myszka, S., Roberts, W. M., Woods, C. T., & Davids, K. (2024).** Applying an ecological approach to practice design in American football: Some case examples on best practice. *Sports Coaching Review, 13*(3), 362–385. [doi:10.1080/21640629.2022.2057698](https://doi.org/10.1080/21640629.2022.2057698) · `key=7M8YQMKU`
  `LIB/yearby-2024-applying-an-ecological-approach-to-practice-design-in-american-football-some-case-examples.md`
  **The single most on-mission paper in the library.** Translates ecological dynamics, representative learning design, and the CLA into two concrete American-football cases. Use for: the whole spine of the course; every worked football example.

- **Myszka, S., Yearby, T., & Davids, K. (2024).** *Being Water*: How key ideas from the practice of Bruce Lee align with contemporary theorizing in movement skill acquisition. *Sport, Education and Society*. [doi:10.1080/13573322.2022.2160701](https://doi.org/10.1080/13573322.2022.2160701)
  `LIB/myszka-2024-i-being-water-i-how-key-ideas-from-the-practice-of-bruce-lee-align-with-contemporary-theor.md`
  Use for: adaptability as the goal rather than a repeatable ideal technique. Good rhetorical ammunition for the coach conversation.

- **Rob Gray — *How We Learn to Move: A Revolution in the Way We Coach & Practice Sports Skills*** (2021). **NOT YET IN THE LIBRARY — acquire.**
  Use for: Joe's primary self-study text. Plain-language introduction to ecological dynamics, the CLA, and differential learning. Pair with the *Perception & Action* podcast back-catalogue.

## Knowledge — The return-to-performance bridge (already in the library)

=====RES 106-192=====
## Knowledge — External, not yet in the library

- **[Perception & Action Podcast](https://perceptionaction.com/) — Rob Gray.** Long back-catalogue; episodes on rehab and the CLA. Use for: Joe's commute listening between lessons.
- **Davids, K., Button, C., & Bennett, S. — *Dynamics of Skill Acquisition: An Ecological Dynamics Approach* (2nd ed.).** [Human Kinetics](https://us.humankinetics.com/products/dynamics-of-skill-acquisition-2nd-edition). The academic root text. Heavier than Gray; reference, not reading.
- **"Anterior Cruciate Ligament Reconstruction Rehabilitation as a Complex Adaptive Process: From Control–Chaos to Actionable Return-to-Sport Decisions."** [PMC12649574](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12649574/). Directly joins Taberner's control-chaos continuum to ecological dynamics. **Strong candidate to ingest into the library next.**

- **Alex Sarama — the constraint-design craft, from basketball.** Investigated 2026-09-02 at Eric's request; site reviewed in full the same day. **Read the framing note first, it decides how to use him.**

  **This entry was written from his website. A 51-minute interview with Rob Gray raised the assessment substantially — see "Gray interviews Sarama (ep 489)" below, which supplies his individualisation method and corrects one claim here.**

  **Framing.** Constraint design is one craft. Whether you are developing a healthy player or returning an injured one, the underlying job is identical: build a task that makes the athlete solve a real problem, and choose which knob to turn. Sarama is a genuine authority on **that craft**. He is not a source on **dosage** — how much chaos this athlete can absorb 12 weeks post-op. **Two different layers, two different sources:**
  - **Sarama answers "what does the task look like, and which constraint do I manipulate?"**
  - **Taberner answers "how much of it can this athlete take today?"** (`C3L296T9`, `JA5QFPKR`, Tier 1 below.)

  Joe is a clinician. He arrives already holding the dosage layer and short on the design layer. **The design layer is the part this course has to teach, and it is the part Sarama is best at.**

  - **Who he is.** British, b. 1995. Head Coach, **Portland Fire (WNBA)**, 2026–. Previously assistant coach / director of player development, **Cleveland Cavaliers** (2024–26, the 64-win season); Rip City Remix; London Lions; Paris Basketball. Clinics in 40+ countries. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Sarama) · [Bio](https://transformingbball.com/staff-bios-alex-sarama) · [ESPN on the Fire's CLA practice](https://www.espn.com/wnba/story/_/id/49364025/wnba-2026-portland-fire-cla-constraints-led-approach-alex-sarama-expansion)
  - **What he has written.** *Transforming Basketball* (2024) — practitioner-facing. 1st ed. self-published (ISBN 9798876624888); 2nd ed., subtitled *A Constraints-Led Approach to Basketball Performance*, is ISBN 9781394454013 — **publisher not verified from here.** **And, more importantly:** *A Constraints-Led Approach to Coaching Basketball*, **Sarama, Lascu, Vaz Rocha & Houghton** — **Routledge**, ISBN 9781032780726, in the *Routledge Studies in Constraints-Based Methodologies in Sport* series — **the same series as Renshaw, Davids, Newcombe & Roberts**. Listed as 2026; his own bio page lists a similarly titled book for 2027. **Confirm it has actually shipped before ordering.** Co-author **Dr Alex Lascu** (PhD, skill acquisition; University of Canberra / Victoria University) is a publishing academic. Placement in that series, plus an academic co-author, puts this a tier above his self-published work.

  ### Where his principles collide with rehab — this is the teachable part

  The [5 principles of the CLA](https://transformingbball.com/constraints-led-approach-the-5-principles/) are free, and **two of them contradict how rehab drills are normally built.** That contradiction is lesson material, not trivia.

  **Byline check (2026-09-02): the two best blog pages are written by *George Vaz*, not by Sarama.** The blog is multi-author — a third page is by Adam De Groot. Vaz is not a guest: he is **George Vaz Rocha, a co-author on the Routledge book**, so this is house material rather than Sarama's personal writing. **Attribute to Vaz, or to Transforming Basketball — not to Sarama.**

  - **Task Simplification — "reduce the problem, but keep perception and action together."** The stated example: do not remove the defender, *reduce the defensive pressure*. **That is the whole of what the source claims** — it is a coaching point about beginners, made with no reference to injury.
    **The rehab extension below is mine, not theirs, and must be labelled that way in any lesson:** the reflex regression in RTP is to strip a task to 1-on-0, which on this logic does not simplify the task but **deletes** it — removing the very perception the returning athlete needs to rebuild. **Strong lesson-0001 rival to the Young 2015 agility hook.** **Do not attribute this extension to Sarama or Vaz.** Cite the peer-reviewed version instead: Parry (2025) on opposed vs unopposed practice (`CA2CRR6Z`).
  - **External Focus of Attention** — cue the effect, not the body part. **Eric already owns the peer-reviewed rehab version of this claim:** Singh, Gokeler & Benjaminse (2021), attentional focus after ACL reconstruction (`EYKZD68B`, Tier 2 below). **Same principle, coaching side and clinical side.** Teach them together — it shows Joe the two literatures are describing one thing.
  - **Functional Variability** — no single correct technique; success is solving the problem, not matching a form model. Converges with the symmetry-metrics caution already noted above: **a movement that looks textbook is not the readiness criterion.**
  - **Representative Learning Design** and **Manipulation of Constraints** — the standard framing, stated plainly. The sharpest line on the page: **if you are constantly yelling instructions, you have a design problem, not an athlete problem.**
  - **The guardrail — over-constraining.** Piling on restrictions until only one solution survives. **Source note: this warning is standard in the wider CLA literature but does NOT appear on the Transforming Basketball 5-principles page** (checked 2026-09-02). Do not cite it to them; cite Renshaw/Davids or the Yearby anchor paper. **Worth teaching anyway, because in rehab it is the live risk** — a heavily constrained "safe" drill can look controlled while quietly removing the problem-solving the athlete came back to rebuild. **That rehab application is an inference, not a sourced claim.**

  ### Free material worth taking (nothing needs buying)

  - **[Newell's constraints, with a practical basketball list](https://transformingbball.com/practical-basketball-constraints/)** — by **George Vaz**; the most useful single page on the site. A worked catalogue sorted by **task** (shot clock, dribble limits, altered scoring, shot-selection rules, closeout type, defender start position), **environment** (music, crowd noise, no talking), and **individual** (fatigue state, opponent size and speed, position-specific bonuses). **This is a ready-made starting schema for the phase-2 drill tool's constraint taxonomy.** Football equivalents have to be written, but the *structure* transfers directly.
  - **[Free activities page](https://transformingbball.com/transforming-activities)** — 10 small-sided games. Honest caveat: they are described loosely, with **no constraint labels, no stated learning aim, no progressions**. Use them to see the shape of a constrained task, not as a model for how to document one. **Note the gap — the drill tool should output what these are missing.**
  - **Blog and the Transforming Basketball podcast** (EP5 on the CLA, EP132 on effective constraint manipulation). **Free on Apple Podcasts and Spotify** — the site's own player is paywalled, so go via Apple or Spotify.

[doi:10.1080/21640629.2022.2158579](https://doi.org/10.1080/21640629.2022.2158579) · [Edinburgh Research Explorer](https://www.research.ed.ac.uk/en/publications/constraints-of-the-constraints-led-approach-in-american-football-/)
  **A direct, peer-reviewed rebuttal to this course's anchor paper (`7M8YQMKU`), in this exact sport, in the same journal.** The authors (University of Edinburgh) accept the CLA is a useful tool but argue that **as a standalone approach it carries mechanistic and epistemological problems that block experimental comparison and limit its novelty and real-world applicability**, and that drawing on a **wider set of theoretical perspectives** serves practitioners better.

### Shawn Myszka — the credentials this file previously understated

Recorded because the practitioners section describes him only as "movement-skill acquisition with NFL players."
**Performance advisor and movement/skill-acquisition specialist to individual NFL players since 2008 — among the first in the United States to apply an ecological approach in American football.** **Over 145 professional football players, including 7 All-Pro selections and 14 Pro Bowl selections.** Pro Performance Director at **Explosive Edge Athletics** (Minneapolis); **co-director of education at Emergence**; advises **a dozen-plus NFL players a year**. Coined the **Movement Problem-Solving Paradigm**. On X as [@MovementMiyagi](https://x.com/movementmiyagi).
**For Joe this matters practically: the football claims in the textbook are backed by seventeen years of NFL casework, not by theory alone.** That is the sentence to use when a coach asks who these people are.

# Yearby et al. 2024 — Ecological practice design in American football

> **Citation**
> Yearby, T., Myszka, S., Roberts, W. M., Woods, C. T., & Davids, K. (2024). Applying an ecological approach to practice design in American football: Some case examples on best practice. *Sports Coaching Review, 13*(3), 362–385. https://doi.org/10.1080/21640629.2022.2057698

## Why it was promoted

This theory-practice paper translates ecological dynamics, representative learning design, and a constraints-led approach into two concrete American-football examples spanning professional and high-school players.

## Research question

What might an ecological-dynamics rationale look, feel, and sound like when designing American-football practice tasks?

## Population and context

- Participants: One NFL defensive end in the first case and groups of 5–12 offensive and defensive high-school players, aged 16–18 years, in the second case.
- Sport and level: American football, from high school through the NFL.
- Training or return-to-play context: Offseason movement-skill preparation and practice design; not rehabilitation.
- Inclusion and exclusion boundaries: Purposively described applied cases from the lead authors' coaching practice rather than a sampled cohort.

## Study design and methods

- Design: Theory-practice paper with two descriptive case examples; no experimental comparison.
- Exposure or intervention: Representative, learner-centred practice tasks created by manipulating individual, environmental, and task constraints.
- Comparator: Conceptual contrast with decontextualized, coach-centred drills; no concurrent control group.
- Measurements and outcomes: Coaches' observations of movement solutions and athletes' comments; no standardized performance, learning, injury, or retention outcome.
- Analysis: Narrative interpretation through ecological dynamics; no prespecified quantitative analysis.

## Key findings

- The NFL defensive-end task retained a centre, offensive tackle, and quarterback so the defender could couple movement to snap and opponent information instead of rehearsing unopposed technique. [p. 15]
- After the offseason case, the authors observed new pass-rush options, including an inside spin, jab-step accelerations, and hand-chop variations, along with more context-specific adaptation. [p. 18]
- The high-school task progressed from one-versus-one open-space tackling to a co-designed five-versus-three run-pass problem with additional positions and changing spatial constraints. [p. 21]
- Across nearly six months, the authors perceived more efficient problem solving as complexity increased, while athletes reported that the game felt slower and that they felt more relaxed. [p. 22]

## Limitations and applicability

- These are illustrative coaching cases, not controlled evaluations; observed changes cannot establish causality or superiority over other practice methods.
- The paper reports no baseline values, objective outcome measures, retention or transfer tests, comparison group, uncertainty estimates, or adverse-event surveillance.
- The authors acknowledge limited American-football-specific applied research and call for more research across performance levels and coach perspectives. [p. 23]
- Contact, fatigue, anxiety, equipment, space, and player-number manipulations change both learning demands and physical risk; implementation requires progressive loading and appropriate medical and coaching safeguards.
- The NFL single-player and one high-school setting do not establish effectiveness across positions, teams, developmental stages, or competition phases.

## Practitioner interpretation

Treat the two cases as design prompts, not validated recipes. Preserve the information that specifies the target football problem, co-design constraints with players and position coaches, and progress opponent presence, space, numbers, equipment, and contact while monitoring physical exposure. Test transfer in the team's own context with predefined football-relevant outcomes.

## Evidence map

| Claim | Locator | Evidence type |
|---|---|---|
| Paper aim and case range | p. 2 | purpose |
| Theory-practice design and authors' applied context | p. 4 | method/context |
| NFL representative task design | p. 15 | case method |
| Observed NFL movement strategies | p. 18 | descriptive observation |
| High-school task progression | p. 21 | case method |
| High-school observations and athlete comments | p. 22 | descriptive observation |
| Need for further research | p. 23 | limitation |

## Related knowledge

- None identified during this bounded review.

# Yearby et al. 2024 — Ecological practice design in American football

> **Citation**
> Yearby, T., Myszka, S., Roberts, W. M., Woods, C. T., & Davids, K. (2024). Applying an ecological approach to practice design in American football: Some case examples on best practice. *Sports Coaching Review, 13*(3), 362–385. https://doi.org/10.1080/21640629.2022.2057698

## Why it was promoted

This theory-practice paper translates ecological dynamics, representative learning design, and a constraints-led approach into two concrete American-football examples spanning professional and high-school players.

## Research question

What might an ecological-dynamics rationale look, feel, and sound like when designing American-football practice tasks?

## Population and context

- Participants: One NFL defensive end in the first case and groups of 5–12 offensive and defensive high-school players, aged 16–18 years, in the second case.
- Sport and level: American football, from high school through the NFL.
- Training or return-to-play context: Offseason movement-skill preparation and practice design; not rehabilitation.
- Inclusion and exclusion boundaries: Purposively described applied cases from the lead authors' coaching practice rather than a sampled cohort.

## Study design and methods

- Design: Theory-practice paper with two descriptive case examples; no experimental comparison.
- Exposure or intervention: Representative, learner-centred practice tasks created by manipulating individual, environmental, and task constraints.
- Comparator: Conceptual contrast with decontextualized, coach-centred drills; no concurrent control group.
- Measurements and outcomes: Coaches' observations of movement solutions and athletes' comments; no standardized performance, learning, injury, or retention outcome.
- Analysis: Narrative interpretation through ecological dynamics; no prespecified quantitative analysis.

## Key findings

- The NFL defensive-end task retained a centre, offensive tackle, and quarterback so the defender could couple movement to snap and opponent information instead of rehearsing unopposed technique. [p. 15]
- After the offseason case, the authors observed new pass-rush options, including an inside spin, jab-step accelerations, and hand-chop variations, along with more context-specific adaptation. [p. 18]
- The high-school task progressed from one-versus-one open-space tackling to a co-designed five-versus-three run-pass problem with additional positions and changing spatial constraints. [p. 21]
- Across nearly six months, the authors perceived more efficient problem solving as complexity increased, while athletes reported that the game felt slower and that they felt more relaxed. [p. 22]

## Limitations and applicability

- These are illustrative coaching cases, not controlled evaluations; observed changes cannot establish causality or superiority over other practice methods.
- The paper reports no baseline values, objective outcome measures, retention or transfer tests, comparison group, uncertainty estimates, or adverse-event surveillance.
- The authors acknowledge limited American-football-specific applied research and call for more research across performance levels and coach perspectives. [p. 23]
- Contact, fatigue, anxiety, equipment, space, and player-number manipulations change both learning demands and physical risk; implementation requires progressive loading and appropriate medical and coaching safeguards.
- The NFL single-player and one high-school setting do not establish effectiveness across positions, teams, developmental stages, or competition phases.

## Practitioner interpretation

Treat the two cases as design prompts, not validated recipes. Preserve the information that specifies the target football problem, co-design constraints with players and position coaches, and progress opponent presence, space, numbers, equipment, and contact while monitoring physical exposure. Test transfer in the team's own context with predefined football-relevant outcomes.

## Evidence map

| Claim | Locator | Evidence type |
|---|---|---|
| Paper aim and case range | p. 2 | purpose |
| Theory-practice design and authors' applied context | p. 4 | method/context |
| NFL representative task design | p. 15 | case method |
| Observed NFL movement strategies | p. 18 | descriptive observation |
| High-school task progression | p. 21 | case method |
| High-school observations and athlete comments | p. 22 | descriptive observation |
| Need for further research | p. 23 | limitation |

## Related knowledge

- None identified during this bounded review.
