=====THEORY 59-120=====
Unopposed practice as an exploratory process The how and why of isolated, unopposed practice is critical for coaches to consider. Contrary to popular application, we suggest that unopposed, isolated technical practice should be viewed as an exploratory instead of a prescriptive process. The efficacy of unopposed, technical practice tasks paired with prescribed, direct instructions about a universally correct way of performing a technique is something to be questioned. Athletes, especially youngsters maturing over different timescales, could still engage in isolated, unopposed practice to explore their coordination potential. The objective here is not to master a specific technique first and then apply it to the game, but to explore many different techniques within their individual action capabilities. Where possible, especially in team training for youth sports, coaches should follow models such as the Foundations for Task Design (see O’Sullivan et al., 2021a) which includes opponents and direction as key information sources in practice activities. In 4 T. E. PARRY ET AL. youth sports such as soccer, practice should consist of interpersonal activities that involve the majority of players and a developmentally appropriate level of opposition. The opposi­ tion in these tasks can be constrained (e.g., defenders arms behind back) to increase the affordances available to the attacking player, increasing success. Such exposure to key sources of perceptual information (opponents) in practice is vital if we are to enhance transfer to competition. However, there could still be a role for unopposed activities in team practice sessions, but they should include an element of unpredictability and variability to enhance transfer to competition. It is important to note that athletes never perform move­ ments separated from a performance environment; their actions are continuously shaped by perceptual information, such as the locations and movements of teammates and opponents (Otte et al., 2021). Therefore, if unopposed practice tasks can include the unpredictable movements of other performers in the same space there is a greater chance of positive transfer to competition. For example, technical “activation” activities at the start of practice can be made more alive, and thus functional, by having athletes perform techniques in the same space. Instead of the commonly used predetermined passing patterns, coaches can design dribbling and passing grids where there are multiple performers operating in the same area (Figures 1 and 2). These more dynamic environments could encourage athletes to seek affordances as they look for space to exploit and gaps to dribble or pass through. During competition, the emergent properties of the situation dictate the functional actions required to be successful, meaning actions are not separate from the perception of relevant information in the environment. Therefore, coaches should try to avoid prescribed drills Figure 1. Dribbling, passing & receiving grid. QUEST 5 Figure 2. Criss-cross passing combination activity. where athletes know the solution ahead of time and instead require them to respond to the emerging opportunities of the task. Figure 1 denotes such an activity where, after receiving the ball, athletes will dribble into emerging space and look to pass to an open teammate on the outside of the grid. As the passer takes the spot of the receiver on the outside of the grid, the receiver then dribbles into the grid and looks to pass to an open teammate, and so on. Figure 2 shows another example of a more alive, unopposed activity that encourages combination passes while two teams operate in the same space. In this activity, teams are not opposing each other or trying to steal the other team’s ball. They are simply adding interference to the task by moving in the same space. The task goal for one team (X’s) is to pass the ball using the middle three players to the other side of the grid in a North-South direction. The task goal for the other team (O’s) is to pass the ball using the middle three players to the other side of the grid in an EastWest direction. A common task rule constraint is to require a minimum of one combina­ tion pass between any of the middle three players before passing to the opposite end target player. Coaches can also add competition by having teams keep score of how many times they successfully transfer the ball to the opposite target player and back. There is no doubt that motivated athletes will want to interact with their sport outside of team practice, often alone at home. Such practice is widely accepted as being fun and beneficial for skill development; however, the intention should not be to perfect certain techniques through rote repetition, for example, passing in soccer, but to explore the multitude of different ways one can do so. If an athlete is home alone, they could still develop skill through individual, exploratory activities. For example, a player can search for 6 T. E. PARRY ET AL. ways to utilize spin on the ball (for shots or passes) by exploring striking it in different ways with different parts of their foot. While teammates, opponents, and other constraints, such as fans and the accompanying pressure and anxiety perceived because of their presence, are not shaping the behavior during this isolated exploration, players can still search for creative ways of moving that could give rise to them performing differently or with more confidence in competition. Ultimately, the key is to allow the athlete an opportunity to experiment with little consequence so they can “explore, search, and discover” potential movement strategies with little pressure to “get it right” so they can move more freely. It is worth noting that there is limited evidence to suggest that unopposed practice must precede opposed, game-like practice. The use of either should be intentionally implemented and relevant to your athletes, avoiding a “copy and paste” method of coaching (O’Sullivan et al., 2023). What is clear though is by exposing athletes to more representative learning environments (e.g., opposed activities), they will become more attuned to important information that guides their decisions and actions in competition (Button et al., 2020). Opposed practice as alive movement problems At a certain level, no two movement problems in sport are ever really the same (Myszka et al., 2023b); in this way, each problem is a highly emergent one, unique from every other that has come before or will come again. Moreover, the concept of aliveness (Lee, 1975) in movement problems begins to capture the true essence of opposed practice. Therefore, we propose that the notion of aliveness is the focal point for coaches in setting forth an effective practice environment for the optimal development of athletes. Alive movement problems are those that are dynamic (i.e., constantly changing moment-to-moment), variable (i.e., differing in some way each time they are faced), and unpredictable (i.e., indeterminate) (Myszka et al., 2023b; Yearby et al., 2024). Because of this, athletes are required to continually (re)organize system degrees of freedom (DoF) (i.e., perceptual, cognitive, and motor/action)1 to functionally fit in with the unfolding problem within the performance environment. Due to their nature, these alive movement problems will consist of deep and rich informational variables that an athlete must become perceptually connected to, enabling them to couple their movement behaviors in close relation to them (Myszka et al., 2023b). In many sports (e.g., rugby, mixed martial arts), the most specifying informational variables (e.g., interpersonal distance, posture/kinematics, relative velocity values) will be directly related to the movement behaviors of another athlete (teammate or opponent; Passos et al., 2008). As Gibson stated, “behavior affords behavior” (Gibson, 1979, p. 135), meaning that how other individuals are moving in an environment will channel the opportunities for all others to behave and perform. Therefore, if opponents are not present in practice environments, as is the case in many traditionally prescribed training drills, athletes will not have the opportunity to perceive and act upon the behaviors of other living, breathing individuals who are also concurrently carrying out movements in dynamic fashions. Thus, whenever possible, it is vital that opposition is present in practice activities to maintain high levels of aliveness, so athletes are able to become more attuned, inten­ tional, and adaptable (Myszka et al., 2023b). Doing so will keep movements coupled to relevant information while embracing the important concepts of context-conditioned variability2 and repetition without repetition (Bernstein, 1967).3 When beginning to assess QUEST 7 the practice activities present within a learning environment, a coach can ask a number of pertinent questions about the nature of the unfoldin

=====FOOTBALL CASE 166-250=====
Case example #2 – enhancing aliveness to develop dexterous players in American football American football is a dynamic sport that requires players to solve emerging problems across various situations and conditions to help their team win games. From the develop­ mental levels to the National Football League (NFL), this has led to coaches searching for and designing practice tasks to assist players in performing skillfully on game day. Unfortunately, many practice tasks fail to capture the complexity of the problems players are asked to solve and instead require them to move in ways that adhere to a prescribed model of movement deemed to be “correct” by a coach as they navigate through passive, unopposed drills (i.e., lacking aliveness). Using a real-life example from when one of the authors consulted with an NFL team, we offer several key practical modifications that were made within football practice environments to enhance aliveness with (and through) the presence of opponents. Further, we include additional changes that could have been made for the running backs, which might be embraced by other interested coaches if they meet the individual needs of their athletes. Individualized skills lead to individualized approaches As discussed earlier, when adopting an ecological dynamics framework, the athleteenvironment relationship is the appropriate scale of analysis for understanding human behavior. Additionally, it is critical for coaches to understand that affordances, while linking the athlete and the environment, will be individual and frame-dependent. For example, when solving a similar unfolding problem on a football field (e.g., an offtackle run), one ball carrier may perceive an affordance to cut back between defenders in the middle of the field, while another may perceive an affordance to bounce the ball to the outside, eluding them by outrunning them to the boundary, highlighting the individual-dependent nature of affordances. Furthermore, when interacting with a comparable problem, the same ball carriers may detect other affordances – highlight­ ing the frame-dependent nature of affordances – and organize different solutions because of the prevailing constraints (e.g., the movement repertoire of the opposing players, field conditions, and the down and distance). Armed with a greater under­ standing of the unfolding interactions and the coalescing constraints that shape them, coaches should consider re-aligning their role toward being a designer of practice tasks (Woods et al., 2021; Yearby et al., 2022) that are filled with various opportunities for interacting based on movement analysis done for each individual. Doing this prior­ itizes the individualized nature of the learners – in this case, American football players – offering them autonomy to search for authentic movement solutions to meet the needs of emerging movement problems (Myszka et al., 2023b). This case example will 12 T. E. PARRY ET AL. Table 1. Individualized player analysis and profiling of two NFL running backs on the same team, each with highly specific strengths, weaknesses, and areas for improvement. Running back #1 ● 6’1”/225lb ● 24 years old, 2nd year in the NFL ● Very powerful and highly explosive (40+” vertical jump and nearly 11-foot broad jump) Strengths: ● In his first NFL season, he displayed glimpses of a high abundance of movement strategies, which may lead to a higher potential for future adaptability (e.g., having access to various cutting strategies, including jump cuts and wider-stance power cuts). ● Able to run a variety of routes proficiently and across the offensive formation (e.g., from the backfield, in the slot, split out wide). Relatedly, modern NFL offenses are attempting to get greater value out of running backs who are able to skillfully run routes by keeping them on the field as “three down backs” to create mismatches versus lesser skilled players. Gaps: ● Frequently gets fixated on the most proximal, immediate defender and thus has a tendency to miss the perceptual pick-up of relevant information sources that lie deeper in the problem as well as opportunities wider across the landscape in his periphery. ● Often sees movement problems through a strength/power lens (e.g., attempts to lower his center of mass in an attempt to “run behind his pads” and run through tackle attempts), which equates to him potentially missing opportunities to make opponents miss (e.g., not sensitive to body posture and kinematics of defenders or interpersonal distance). Specific Areas for Improvement: ● Help him gain comfort in more chaos so he’s able to move at “ownership speeds”, which could (in theory) allow him to better coordinate and control the most functional movement solution to the peculiar problem (e.g., perceiving/ acting on simultaneous and successive affordances in relation to teammate-opponent interactions). ● Increase his perceptual attunement, which could lead to his ability to solve more complex movement problems and string together more adaptable moves in relation to the unfolding problem (e.g., detecting information about affordances presented in tight traffic situations). Running back #2 ● 5’11”/195lb ● 30 years old, 9th year in the NFL ● Former NFL All-Pro and NFL single-season rushing champion ● One of the fastest players at his position in the history of the NFL Strengths: ● He is able to perceive while moving at high speeds, but still has gaps related to this (see below). ● He has the ability to contort his body in unique positions and frequently displays rapid footwork, deceleration, and variable evasive cutting strategies. ● He can be used, play-to-play, in highly versatile ways due to his vast experience and exposure to diverse problems (across situations and positions). Gaps: ● Often sees movement problems through an acceleration/speed lens (e.g., feels like he can win versus opponents by simply outrunning them). ● Based on age and wear and tear due to the high number of snaps played in his career, his physical characteristics, namely those related to his former world-class football acceleration and speed, have begun to diminish dramatically. ● When he tries to make opponents miss in evasive agility situations, he will occasionally execute what appears to be a predetermined move, which leads to him carrying out movement solutions that are not fit for the problem (i.e., lacking functionality). Specific Areas for Improvement: ● Because of decreases in his acceleration and speed capabilities over the past several seasons, he has struggled to perceptually pick up informational variables in unfolding interactions (e.g., relative velocity values or angles between him and the nearest opponent), so it will be important to give him more opportunities to explore how to couple his movement behaviors directly to his opponent’s (i.e., calibration). ● Encourage him to explore potentially novel, creative, and authentic movement solutions in situations where he is highly accustomed to relying on movement strategies that were formerly effective. be used to illustrate how detailed movement analysis was done for two of the team’s running backs (see Table 1) to assist in designing effective learning environments. The profiling provided in the accompanying table is meant to serve as an overview of the more detailed, extensive movement and skill execution analysis that was provided to the team. QUEST 13 What football coaches may prescribe For a number of examples of the types of drills that football coaches may be likely to use in practice for the training of running backs, we point to a previous video released by USA Football (2014),5 highlighting an “individual” practice period for the Miami Dolphins of the NFL. As readers may note, these activities (i.e., cone drills) bear little resemblance to the highly alive movement problems that are presented to running backs immersed in compe­ titive demands; they simply do not contain the relevant information that players will utilize to coordinate their movement solutions (Passos et al., 2013, 2011). Nevertheless, these drills are commonplace in many NFL and American football practice environments. Behavior affords behavior: modifying practice activities by adding opposition There are several practice activities commonly used by coaches at the NFL level (including the team that one of the authors consulted with) that could be adjusted slightly, namely through the inclusion of opposition, to more effectively target the movement skills needed for running backs while also addressing specific player needs. Figures 5 and 6 are modified activities that were used for each player (i.e., the team’s #1 and #2 running backs) based on a detailed analysis of their individual movement skill sets, followed by two tasks (see Figures 7 and 8) that were used to help all running backs adapt their skills. Before describing the Figure 5. This activity is designed for running backs, who are offensive players (listed as RB in each figure), to develop a functional fit in relation to a teammate’s (represented by the letter X) block on an opponent (i.e., defensive players, who are represented by the letter O in each figure), while simulta­ neously remaining attuned to the movement behaviors of a free defender. Please note, and we emphasize, that while this figure and the following three (i.e., Figures 6–8) are presented statically, in practice, the movement problems are alive and replete with opportunities for interaction. Dashed lines are used for both sides of the ball in this figure and the following three to illustrate the indeterminate way of behaving. 14 T. E. PARRY ET AL. Figure 6. This activity is designed for running backs to work on adapting their own movement strategies to the changing angles and speeds of an immediate opponent. Figure 7. This activity is designed for running backs to develop elusiveness versus multiple opponents in the open field while operating in a tunnel. QUEST 15 Figure 8. This activity is designed for running backs to work on perceiving and acting upon the affordances of dynamically changing gaps emerging from the interactions between teammates and defenders. practice tasks, it is important to identify who the individuals are that could be involved in the training activities. Ideally, coaches would pair two or more position groups together (e.g., running backs and linebackers), which provides both parties with an opportunity to solve changing movement problems in relation to one another (behavior affords behavior; Gibson, 1979). If that is not feasible, the next best option would be having a player (or several, depending on the task) of the same position group “play” the other side of the ball (e.g., a defensive back acts as the wide receiver). If players are not an option, coaches could play the role of the opposition—while they may not move as skillfully, their presence still presents alive movement problems for the players to solve. It should be mentioned that there are some teams that have “crossover indy periods,” which is a positive first step in creating learning environments where players are offered the opportunity to find functional solutions to emerging problems. Fit work in relation to a teammate The first task, which is commonly used in more prescriptive ways with little to no room for exploration, was modified for the #1 running back in efforts to assist them in learning to “read and react” off of a teammate’s block (e.g., a tight end or wide receiver) coupled with the behavior of one or more defenders (see Figure 5). # Rob Gray's free infographics — local copies

**Saved 2026-09-03** from [perceptionaction.com](https://perceptionaction.com/), index page
[/resources/](https://perceptionaction.com/resources/).

`NOTES.md` said to take local copies because it is one person's website and the material is
free but not archived anywhere else. This is that.

**All images are the full-resolution originals**, not the 1024px versions the site displays.
The `-1024x576` suffix WordPress appends was stripped to reach the source file.

## What is here

| File | What it is | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| `comparative-training-studies.md` | **21 head-to-head training studies**, traditional vs ecological, extracted to a searchable table | **The page Joe brings when someone pushes back.** Evidence, not philosophy. |
| `two-approaches.md` + `.jpg` | Information-processing vs ecological, side by side. Transcribed from the image. | Lets Joe state the view he disagrees with, fairly. See the note on the last row. |
| `cla.jpg` | Constraints-Led Approach infographic | The core diagram of the whole course. |
| `sports-injury.jpg` | Ecological approach to sports injury | **The most on-mission of the images** — injury is the workspace's whole subject. |
| `differential-learning.jpg` | Differential Learning | Background. DL is not the CLA; keep them distinct. |
| `variability-of-practice.jpg` | Variability of Practice | Feeds the "no single correct technique" argument. |
| `direct-learning.jpg` | Direct Learning | Background theory. |
| `*.html` | The source pages as served | Kept so the extractions can be re-checked against the original. |

## Two rows worth pulling into lesson 0001

Both land on the opposed/unopposed argument from independent directions:

- **`two-approaches.md`, last row** — *Modularity / Separability / Decomposition* versus
  *Coupling / Inseparability / Simplification*. Removing the defender is decomposition. The
  ecological claim is that you cannot take perception and action apart.
- **`comparative-training-studies.md`, study 17** — Caldeira et al. (2023), volleyball.
  **Task simplification beat task decomposition** in a head-to-head. That is the exact
  distinction, tested, with a result.

Also note **studies 9 and 18** (Orangi et al., 2021a and 2023): both CLA and DL lowered ACL
injury risk factors, with larger effects for CLA. **Those are the two rows a physician will
care about.**

## Handling

Gray's material, free and public, saved here for internal study only. **Do not republish
and do not commit.** When a claim from these goes into a lesson, cite the underlying study —
not the infographic and not this folder.

## Re-fetching

The script that built this folder is disposable and lives in the job tmp dir. To rebuild:
download each page listed on [/resources/](https://perceptionaction.com/resources/), strip
the `-NNNxNNN` suffix from image URLs to get the original, and re-extract the tables.
Watch for two traps found on 2026-09-03:

1. The site's WordPress **calendar widget is a `<table>`** and gets scraped as content.
2. The Two Approaches graphic is listed on `/resources/` next to the terminology video, so
   it is easy to mislabel as that video's thumbnail. **It is not.** It is the infographic.

=====THEORY 59-120=====
Unopposed practice as an exploratory process The how and why of isolated, unopposed practice is critical for coaches to consider. Contrary to popular application, we suggest that unopposed, isolated technical practice should be viewed as an exploratory instead of a prescriptive process. The efficacy of unopposed, technical practice tasks paired with prescribed, direct instructions about a universally correct way of performing a technique is something to be questioned. Athletes, especially youngsters maturing over different timescales, could still engage in isolated, unopposed practice to explore their coordination potential. The objective here is not to master a specific technique first and then apply it to the game, but to explore many different techniques within their individual action capabilities. Where possible, especially in team training for youth sports, coaches should follow models such as the Foundations for Task Design (see O’Sullivan et al., 2021a) which includes opponents and direction as key information sources in practice activities. In 4 T. E. PARRY ET AL. youth sports such as soccer, practice should consist of interpersonal activities that involve the majority of players and a developmentally appropriate level of opposition. The opposi­ tion in these tasks can be constrained (e.g., defenders arms behind back) to increase the affordances available to the attacking player, increasing success. Such exposure to key sources of perceptual information (opponents) in practice is vital if we are to enhance transfer to competition. However, there could still be a role for unopposed activities in team practice sessions, but they should include an element of unpredictability and variability to enhance transfer to competition. It is important to note that athletes never perform move­ ments separated from a performance environment; their actions are continuously shaped by perceptual information, such as the locations and movements of teammates and opponents (Otte et al., 2021). Therefore, if unopposed practice tasks can include the unpredictable movements of other performers in the same space there is a greater chance of positive transfer to competition. For example, technical “activation” activities at the start of practice can be made more alive, and thus functional, by having athletes perform techniques in the same space. Instead of the commonly used predetermined passing patterns, coaches can design dribbling and passing grids where there are multiple performers operating in the same area (Figures 1 and 2). These more dynamic environments could encourage athletes to seek affordances as they look for space to exploit and gaps to dribble or pass through. During competition, the emergent properties of the situation dictate the functional actions required to be successful, meaning actions are not separate from the perception of relevant information in the environment. Therefore, coaches should try to avoid prescribed drills Figure 1. Dribbling, passing & receiving grid. QUEST 5 Figure 2. Criss-cross passing combination activity. where athletes know the solution ahead of time and instead require them to respond to the emerging opportunities of the task. Figure 1 denotes such an activity where, after receiving the ball, athletes will dribble into emerging space and look to pass to an open teammate on the outside of the grid. As the passer takes the spot of the receiver on the outside of the grid, the receiver then dribbles into the grid and looks to pass to an open teammate, and so on. Figure 2 shows another example of a more alive, unopposed activity that encourages combination passes while two teams operate in the same space. In this activity, teams are not opposing each other or trying to steal the other team’s ball. They are simply adding interference to the task by moving in the same space. The task goal for one team (X’s) is to pass the ball using the middle three players to the other side of the grid in a North-South direction. The task goal for the other team (O’s) is to pass the ball using the middle three players to the other side of the grid in an EastWest direction. A common task rule constraint is to require a minimum of one combina­ tion pass between any of the middle three players before passing to the opposite end target player. Coaches can also add competition by having teams keep score of how many times they successfully transfer the ball to the opposite target player and back. There is no doubt that motivated athletes will want to interact with their sport outside of team practice, often alone at home. Such practice is widely accepted as being fun and beneficial for skill development; however, the intention should not be to perfect certain techniques through rote repetition, for example, passing in soccer, but to explore the multitude of different ways one can do so. If an athlete is home alone, they could still develop skill through individual, exploratory activities. For example, a player can search for 6 T. E. PARRY ET AL. ways to utilize spin on the ball (for shots or passes) by exploring striking it in different ways with different parts of their foot. While teammates, opponents, and other constraints, such as fans and the accompanying pressure and anxiety perceived because of their presence, are not shaping the behavior during this isolated exploration, players can still search for creative ways of moving that could give rise to them performing differently or with more confidence in competition. Ultimately, the key is to allow the athlete an opportunity to experiment with little consequence so they can “explore, search, and discover” potential movement strategies with little pressure to “get it right” so they can move more freely. It is worth noting that there is limited evidence to suggest that unopposed practice must precede opposed, game-like practice. The use of either should be intentionally implemented and relevant to your athletes, avoiding a “copy and paste” method of coaching (O’Sullivan et al., 2023). What is clear though is by exposing athletes to more representative learning environments (e.g., opposed activities), they will become more attuned to important information that guides their decisions and actions in competition (Button et al., 2020). Opposed practice as alive movement problems At a certain level, no two movement problems in sport are ever really the same (Myszka et al., 2023b); in this way, each problem is a highly emergent one, unique from every other that has come before or will come again. Moreover, the concept of aliveness (Lee, 1975) in movement problems begins to capture the true essence of opposed practice. Therefore, we propose that the notion of aliveness is the focal point for coaches in setting forth an effective practice environment for the optimal development of athletes. Alive movement problems are those that are dynamic (i.e., constantly changing moment-to-moment), variable (i.e., differing in some way each time they are faced), and unpredictable (i.e., indeterminate) (Myszka et al., 2023b; Yearby et al., 2024). Because of this, athletes are required to continually (re)organize system degrees of freedom (DoF) (i.e., perceptual, cognitive, and motor/action)1 to functionally fit in with the unfolding problem within the performance environment. Due to their nature, these alive movement problems will consist of deep and rich informational variables that an athlete must become perceptually connected to, enabling them to couple their movement behaviors in close relation to them (Myszka et al., 2023b). In many sports (e.g., rugby, mixed martial arts), the most specifying informational variables (e.g., interpersonal distance, posture/kinematics, relative velocity values) will be directly related to the movement behaviors of another athlete (teammate or opponent; Passos et al., 2008). As Gibson stated, “behavior affords behavior” (Gibson, 1979, p. 135), meaning that how other individuals are moving in an environment will channel the opportunities for all others to behave and perform. Therefore, if opponents are not present in practice environments, as is the case in many traditionally prescribed training drills, athletes will not have the opportunity to perceive and act upon the behaviors of other living, breathing individuals who are also concurrently carrying out movements in dynamic fashions. Thus, whenever possible, it is vital that opposition is present in practice activities to maintain high levels of aliveness, so athletes are able to become more attuned, inten­ tional, and adaptable (Myszka et al., 2023b). Doing so will keep movements coupled to relevant information while embracing the important concepts of context-conditioned variability2 and repetition without repetition (Bernstein, 1967).3 When beginning to assess QUEST 7 the practice activities present within a learning environment, a coach can ask a number of pertinent questions about the nature of the unfoldin

Case example #2 – enhancing aliveness to develop dexterous players in American football American football is a dynamic sport that requires players to solve emerging problems across various situations and conditions to help their team win games. From the develop­ mental levels to the National Football League (NFL), this has led to coaches searching for and designing practice tasks to assist players in performing skillfully on game day. Unfortunately, many practice tasks fail to capture the complexity of the problems players are asked to solve and instead require them to move in ways that adhere to a prescribed model of movement deemed to be “correct” by a coach as they navigate through passive, unopposed drills (i.e., lacking aliveness). Using a real-life example from when one of the authors consulted with an NFL team, we offer several key practical modifications that were made within football practice environments to enhance aliveness with (and through) the presence of opponents. Further, we include additional changes that could have been made for the running backs, which might be embraced by other interested coaches if they meet the individual needs of their athletes. Individualized skills lead to individualized approaches As discussed earlier, when adopting an ecological dynamics framework, the athleteenvironment relationship is the appropriate scale of analysis for understanding human behavior. Additionally, it is critical for coaches to understand that affordances, while linking the athlete and the environment, will be individual and frame-dependent. For example, when solving a similar unfolding problem on a football field (e.g., an offtackle run), one ball carrier may perceive an affordance to cut back between defenders in the middle of the field, while another may perceive an affordance to bounce the ball to the outside, eluding them by outrunning them to the boundary, highlighting the individual-dependent nature of affordances. Furthermore, when interacting with a comparable problem, the same ball carriers may detect other affordances – highlight­ ing the frame-dependent nature of affordances – and organize different solutions because of the prevailing constraints (e.g., the movement repertoire of the opposing players, field conditions, and the down and distance). # Rob Gray's free infographics — local copies

**Saved 2026-09-03** from [perceptionaction.com](https://perceptionaction.com/), index page
[/resources/](https://perceptionaction.com/resources/).

`NOTES.md` said to take local copies because it is one person's website and the material is
free but not archived anywhere else. This is that.

**All images are the full-resolution originals**, not the 1024px versions the site displays.
The `-1024x576` suffix WordPress appends was stripped to reach the source file.

## What is here

| File | What it is | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| `comparative-training-studies.md` | **21 head-to-head training studies**, traditional vs ecological, extracted to a searchable table | **The page Joe brings when someone pushes back.** Evidence, not philosophy. |
| `two-approaches.md` + `.jpg` | Information-processing vs ecological, side by side. Transcribed from the image. | Lets Joe state the view he disagrees with, fairly. See the note on the last row. |
| `cla.jpg` | Constraints-Led Approach infographic | The core diagram of the whole course. |
| `sports-injury.jpg` | Ecological approach to sports injury | **The most on-mission of the images** — injury is the workspace's whole subject. |
| `differential-learning.jpg` | Differential Learning | Background. DL is not the CLA; keep them distinct. |
| `variability-of-practice.jpg` | Variability of Practice | Feeds the "no single correct technique" argument. |
| `direct-learning.jpg` | Direct Learning | Background theory. |
| `*.html` | The source pages as served | Kept so the extractions can be re-checked against the original. |

## Two rows worth pulling into lesson 0001

Both land on the opposed/unopposed argument from independent directions:

- **`two-approaches.md`, last row** — *Modularity / Separability / Decomposition* versus
  *Coupling / Inseparability / Simplification*. Removing the defender is decomposition. The
  ecological claim is that you cannot take perception and action apart.
- **`comparative-training-studies.md`, study 17** — Caldeira et al. (2023), volleyball.
  **Task simplification beat task decomposition** in a head-to-head. That is the exact
  distinction, tested, with a result.

Also note **studies 9 and 18** (Orangi et al., 2021a and 2023): both CLA and DL lowered ACL
injury risk factors, with larger effects for CLA. **Those are the two rows a physician will
care about.**

## Handling

Gray's material, free and public, saved here for internal study only. **Do not republish
and do not commit.** When a claim from these goes into a lesson, cite the underlying study —
not the infographic and not this folder.

## Re-fetching

The script that built this folder is disposable and lives in the job tmp dir. To rebuild:
download each page listed on [/resources/](https://perceptionaction.com/resources/), strip
the `-NNNxNNN` suffix from image URLs to get the original, and re-extract the tables.
Watch for two traps found on 2026-09-03:

1. The site's WordPress **calendar widget is a `<table>`** and gets scraped as content.
2. The Two Approaches graphic is listed on `/resources/` next to the terminology video, so
   it is easy to mislabel as that video's thumbnail. **It is not.** It is the infographic.

# Learning Record Format

Learning records live in `./learning-records/` and use sequential numbering: `0001-slug.md`, `0002-slug.md`, etc. Create the directory lazily — only when the first record is written.

They are the teaching equivalent of ADRs: they capture non-obvious lessons, key insights, and stated prior knowledge that will steer future sessions. They are used to calculate the zone of proximal development.

## Template

```md
# {Short title of what was learned or established}

{1-3 sentences: what was learned (or what prior knowledge was established), and why it matters for future sessions.}
```

That is the whole format. A learning record can be a single paragraph. The value is recording _that_ this is now known and _why_ it changes what to teach next — not in filling out sections.

## Optional sections

Only include these when they add genuine value. Most records won't need them.

- **Status** frontmatter (`active | superseded by LR-NNNN`) — useful when an earlier understanding turns out to be wrong and is replaced.
- **Evidence** — how the user demonstrated the understanding (a question answered, an exercise completed, prior experience cited). Useful when the claim might be revisited.
- **Implications** — what this unlocks or rules out for future sessions. Worth recording when non-obvious.

## Numbering

Scan `./learning-records/` for the highest existing number and increment by one.

## When to write a learning record

Write one when any of these is true:

1. **The user demonstrated genuine understanding of something non-trivial** — not just exposure, but evidence they can use the concept correctly. This sets a new floor for what to teach next.
2. **The user disclosed prior knowledge** — "I already know X." Record it so future sessions don't re-teach it. Also record the _depth_ claimed.
3. **A misconception was corrected** — the user previously believed something wrong and now sees why. These are high-value: they predict future stumbling blocks for related topics.
4. **The mission shifted in response to learning** — the user discovered they cared about something different than they thought. Cross-link to [[MISSION.md]] and update it.

### What does _not_ qualify

- Material that was merely covered. Coverage is not learning. Wait for evidence.
- Anything already captured tersely in [[GLOSSARY.md]] as a term definition. Don't duplicate.
- Session-by-session activity logs. Learning records are not a journal — they are decision-grade insights.

## Supersession

When a later record contradicts an earlier one (the user's understanding deepened or corrected), mark the old record `Status: superseded by LR-NNNN` rather than deleting it. The history of how understanding evolved is itself useful signal.

10.5040/9781718219342.ch-006 | Blocking | ['Volleyball Fundamentals'] | [] | [[2108]]
10.31979/etd.z2yk-pnu3 | A biomechanical analysis of three blocking footwork patterns in volleyball players | [''] | ['Wanderer'] | [[None]]

Constraints-led return to performance · Lesson 0001

The drill that hid the deficit

Why a drill with no opponent cannot tell you an athlete is ready, what the opponent actually adds, and one sentence you can say to someone who was not there.

About 40 minutes the way you work: read once, take notes, do the quiz, then plan the field task.
Grounded in MISSION.md and the key-answers digest of your 3 September interview. Cheat sheet: reference/0001-opposed-vs-unopposed.

1. Start with a case you already own

In the interview you described a returning offensive lineman with a target game. You ran a needs assessment, worked a reverse calendar back from the game, and built run-blocking days, pass-blocking days and a reaction day. That method stays.

Then this happened. In the non-reactive drills he looked strong. He was experienced enough to time them up. In the reactive pass drills his performance dropped and he reported more strain. And at the end you could not load him at your own size, so a position coach and real defensive-line bodies had to finish the job.

You made a constraints argument without the vocabulary for it. This lesson gives you the vocabulary, one peer-reviewed paper to stand on, and a sentence you can say to a physician or a coordinator who was not at practice.

The belief this lesson corrects

“He looked clean in the pre-set pass drill, so he is ready.” A clean rep in a drill with no opponent shows he can execute a plan he already knows. It does not show he can football.

2. What the opponent is: information

Parry, Myszka, Yearby, O Sullivan and Otte (2025) put it in one line borrowed from Gibson: behavior affords behavior. How the other person moves is what shapes what the athlete can do next. In contact and invasion sports, the most useful information is tied to another body: the distance between them, his posture, how fast the gap is closing.

Parry, T. E., Myszka, S., Yearby, T., O Sullivan, M., & Otte, F. (2025). The value of opposed and unopposed practice: An ecological dynamics rationale for skill development. Quest, 1–21. doi:10.1080/00336297.2024.2420759 — pp. 6–7. The Gibson line is The Ecological Approach to Visual Perception (1979), p. 135, as quoted there.

Now put that on a pass set. The lineman’s job is to pick up the rusher’s first step, his lean, the closing distance, and to set and re-anchor against it as it changes. Take the rusher away and there is nothing to pick up. The lineman sets to a plan instead. He can time it. That is why he looked strong. The drill did not lie to you. It just could not measure the thing you needed to know.

Parry and colleagues say it plainly: if opponents are not present, athletes “will not have the opportunity to perceive and act upon the behaviors of other living, breathing individuals” (p. 7). What is missing from the unopposed drill is not effort or load. It is the information the job runs on.

3. Two words, and two ways to make a drill easier

Unopposed practice isolates a skill and repeats it with no opponent present. Opposed practice keeps an opponent in the task, so the problem is alive: it changes moment to moment, it differs each time, and it cannot be fully predicted (Parry et al., 2025, pp. 2, 6). Those two words are the first glossary candidates in this course. Use them at practice this week.

Here is the part that changes how you regress a drill. There are two ways to make a task easier, and they are not the same.

MoveWhat you doWhat happens to the information
DecomposeTake a piece out. No rusher. Bag instead of a body. Cones instead of a defender.Gone. The athlete solves a different, smaller problem.
SimplifyKeep the whole problem. Turn the pressure down. Rusher at half speed, hands behind his back, scripted first step.Still there. The athlete solves the real problem at a lower level.

Parry and colleagues give the second move directly: opposition “can be constrained (e.g., defenders arms behind back) to increase the affordances available to the attacking player, increasing success” (p. 4). Rob Gray draws the same line between the two schools of coaching, decomposition on one side and simplification on the other; his table of comparative studies lists one head-to-head in volleyball where simplification beat decomposition. Treat that row as a pointer, not a citation, until the paper has been read.

Gray, R. Two Approaches and Comparative Training Studies infographics, perceptionaction.com. Local copies: two-approaches.md (last row) and comparative-training-studies.md (study 17, Caldeira et al. 2023, volleyball). The comparative table is the page to bring when someone pushes back.
This course’s extension, not the paper’s

In return to performance the reflex regression is to strip the drill to no opponent. On the logic above that does not simplify the task. It deletes it, and it deletes exactly the perception the returning athlete has to rebuild. Parry et al. write about skill development, not rehabilitation. Applying it to return to performance is our step, and you should say so when you cite it.

4. What the paper does not say

It does not say “never unopposed.” Read it fairly, because the first physician who has read it will.

  • Unopposed work has a place as exploration: a chance to search many ways of moving with little consequence, not to perfect one technique by repetition (pp. 3–6).
  • Unopposed drills can be made alive by putting other moving bodies in the same space, even when nobody is defending anyone (pp. 4–5).
  • There is “limited evidence to suggest that unopposed practice must precede opposed, game-like practice” (p. 6). The ladder you were taught is a habit, not a finding.

So the claim you can defend is narrower and stronger than “opposed is better.” It is this: an unopposed drill is not evidence of readiness, because the information the athlete times up is the information that is missing. Use unopposed work to build capacity and to explore. Do not use it to prove anything.

No opponentBodies in the spaceOpponent, pressure downLive opponent

Readiness lives on the right half of that bar. Regress along it. Do not jump off it.

5. Football, on tape

The course’s anchor paper has the closest case to yours. Yearby, Myszka, Roberts, Woods and Davids (2024) worked with an NFL defensive end in the off-season. Instead of unopposed pass-rush technique, the task kept a centre, an offensive tackle and a quarterback on the field, so the rusher had to couple his movement to the snap and to the tackle’s set (p. 15). Over the off-season they saw new options emerge: an inside spin, jab-step accelerations, hand-chop variations (p. 18). Nobody taught those moves. The opponent did.

Yearby, T., Myszka, S., Roberts, W. M., Woods, C. T., & Davids, K. (2024). Applying an ecological approach to practice design in American football: Some case examples on best practice. Sports Coaching Review, 13(3), 362–385. doi:10.1080/21640629.2022.2057698. Free full text: Sheffield Hallam repository. Case observations, not a controlled trial.

Parry and colleagues do the same for running backs (pp. 11–16). A common “fit off the block” drill, usually run as a script, was rebuilt with a real blocker and a real defender, and then varied by changing who the opponent is, where each player starts, how big the space is, and whether a second defender pursues from depth. The cone drills they contrast it with, they say, “simply do not contain the relevant information that players will utilize” (p. 13).

A weekly habit worth starting: Shawn Myszka breaks down one NFL play a week as a movement problem at Football Beyond The Stats. Watch one, name the problem, name one constraint that would recreate it.

6. When you are not the right constraint

You said it yourself: you cannot load a lineman at your own size. Parry and colleagues give a ladder for who plays the opponent (p. 15):

  1. Pair two position groups. Offensive line against defensive line. Both sides get a live problem.
  2. Same position, other side of the ball. A second lineman plays the rusher.
  3. A coach as the opponent. Less skilled, but “their presence still presents alive movement problems.”

Bringing in the position coach and defensive-line bodies was step one on that ladder. It was the right call. Now it has a name and a citation, and you can say it before someone asks why an athletic trainer needed the defensive line.

One more tool for the safety question, from a practitioner rather than a paper: scripted start, live finish. Fix how the rep begins so exposure is controlled; leave how it ends open so the perception stays. Alex Sarama, in interview with Rob Gray (Perception & Action Podcast, ep. 489). Practitioner opinion, cited as such.

7. The sentence for someone who was not there

This is the thing you said you were least confident about: defending a subjective call to an objective audience. Ask three questions of any drill you want to use as evidence.

  1. What information did he have to pick up?
  2. What did he have to do with it?
  3. How much pressure was it under?

If the answer to the first question is “nothing,” the drill is not evidence. It may still be useful. It is not evidence.

Template

“He had to read [the rusher’s first step and lean] and [set and re-anchor against it] with the rusher at [half speed, hands behind his back]. He did that in five of six reps. The pre-set drill could not show me that, because there was nothing in it to read.”

Those three questions are this course’s framing, built on Parry et al. They are not a quotation. The paper says a coach can ask “a number of pertinent questions” about a drill (p. 7); these are ours.

8. Check yourself

Answer from memory before you scroll back. Wrong answers come with the fix.

A returning lineman looks strong in a pre-set pass drill with no rusher. What does that result tell you?

You want to keep the rusher but make the task easier. Which change keeps the information in the drill?

According to Parry and colleagues, unopposed practice…

9. At practice tomorrow

Field task, with your current returning athlete
  1. Pick one unopposed drill already in his plan.
  2. Write one line: what information is missing from it? Use question one.
  3. Add one opponent with the pressure turned down. Pick one: half speed, hands behind his back, or scripted start with a live finish.
  4. Watch five or six reps. Change nothing while you watch.
  5. Write one line: what did you see that the unopposed drill could not show?

Stay inside whatever he is already cleared for. This changes what the drill shows you, not how far along he is. If the opposed version would load him harder than the drill it replaces, turn the pressure down further, or check with Jacob or Tim first. Bring both lines to lesson 0002.

Primary source for this lesson

Parry, Myszka, Yearby, O Sullivan & Otte (2025). The value of opposed and unopposed practice. Quest. doi:10.1080/00336297.2024.2420759. Read pages 3–7 for the argument and 11–17 for the football case. The journal is paywalled; the PDF is in Eric’s Zotero, item key CA2CRR6Z. Two of the five authors wrote the football textbook this course is built on.

Free tonight: Yearby et al. (2024), the anchor paper, at the Sheffield Hallam repository. Start at the defensive-end case.

Cheat sheet for this lesson: reference/0001-opposed-vs-unopposed.html. Print it.

Anything unclear, or a case this does not fit? Open this folder and ask. The agent that wrote this lesson is your teacher between sessions and can go back to the sources with you.

TermMeaning

An unopposed drill is not evidence of readiness, because the information the athlete times up is exactly the information that is missing. Football runs on reading another body: distance, posture, closing speed.

Two ways to make a drill easier

MoveDoInformation
DecomposeRemove the opponent. Bag, cones, air.Deleted
SimplifyKeep the opponent. Half speed. Hands behind back. Scripted start, live finish.Kept

Regress by simplifying. In return to performance, stripping to no opponent is this course’s named trap, not a finding from the paper.

No opponentBodies in the spaceOpponent, pressure downLive opponent

Readiness is measured on the right half. Move along the bar. Do not jump off it.

1 2 3 4 5 6 Lesson 0001 — The drill that hid the deficit 7 8 9 10 11

Constraints-led return to performance · Lesson 0001

12

The drill that hid the deficit

13

Why a drill with no opponent cannot tell you an athlete is ready, what the opponent actually adds, and one sentence you can say to someone who was not there.

14 15
16 About 40 minutes the way you work: read once, take notes, do the quiz, then plan the field task.
17 Grounded in MISSION.md and the 18 key-answers digest of your 3 September interview. 19 Cheat sheet: reference/0001-opposed-vs-unopposed. 20
21 22

1. Start with a case you already own

23 24

In the interview you described a returning offensive lineman with a target game. You ran a needs assessment, worked a reverse calendar back from the game, and built run-blocking days, pass-blocking days and a reaction day. That method stays.

25 26

Then this happened. In the non-reactive drills he looked strong. He was experienced enough to time them up. In the reactive pass drills his performance dropped and he reported more strain. And at the end you could not load him at your own size, so a position coach and real defensive-line bodies had to finish the job.

27 28

You made a constraints argument without the vocabulary for it. This lesson gives you the vocabulary, one peer-reviewed paper to stand on, and a sentence you can say to a physician or a coordinator who was not at practice.

29 30
31 The belief this lesson corrects 32

“He looked clean in the pre-set pass drill, so he is ready.” A clean rep in a drill with no opponent shows he can execute a plan he already knows. It does not show he can play football.

33
34 35

2. What the opponent is: information

36 37

Parry, Myszka, Yearby, O Sullivan and Otte (2025) put it in one line borrowed from Gibson: behavior affords behavior. How the other person moves is what shapes what the athlete can do next. In contact and invasion sports, the most useful information is tied to another body: the distance between them, his posture, how fast the gap is closing.

38 39
40 Parry, T. E., Myszka, S., Yearby, T., O Sullivan, M., & Otte, F. (2025). The value of opposed and unopposed practice: An ecological dynamics rationale for skill development. Quest, 1–21. doi:10.1080/00336297.2024.2420759 — pp. 6–7. The Gibson line is The Ecological Approach to Visual Perception (1979), p. 135, as quoted there. 41
42 43

Now put that on a pass set. The lineman’s job is to pick up the rusher’s first step, his lean, the closing distance, and to set and re-anchor against it as it changes. Take the rusher away and there is nothing to pick up. The lineman sets to a plan instead. He can time it. That is why he looked strong. The drill did not lie to you. It just could not measure the thing you needed to know.

44 45

Parry and colleagues say it plainly: if opponents are not present, athletes “will not have the opportunity to perceive and act upon the behaviors of other living, breathing individuals” (p. 6). What is missing from the unopposed drill is not effort or load. It is the information the job runs on.

46 47

3. Two words, and two ways to make a drill easier

48 49

Unopposed practice isolates a skill and repeats it with no opponent present. Opposed practice keeps an opponent in the task, so the problem is alive: it changes moment to moment, it differs each time, and it cannot be fully predicted (Parry et al., 2025, pp. 2, 6). Those two words are the first glossary candidates in this course. Use them at practice this week.

50 51

Here is the part that changes how you regress a drill. There are two ways to make a task easier, and they are not the same.

52 53 54 55 56 57 58 59
MoveWhat you doWhat happens to the information
DecomposeTake a piece out. No rusher. Bag instead of a body. Cones instead of a defender.Gone. The athlete solves a different, smaller problem.
SimplifyKeep the whole problem. Turn the pressure down. Rusher at half speed, hands behind his back, scripted first step.Still there. The athlete solves the real problem at a lower level.
60 61

Parry and colleagues give the second move directly: opposition “can be constrained (e.g., defenders arms behind back) to increase the affordances available to the attacking player, increasing success” (p. 4). Rob Gray draws the same line between the two schools of coaching, decomposition on one side and simplification on the other; his table of comparative studies lists one head-to-head in volleyball where simplification beat decomposition. Treat that row as a pointer, not a citation, until the paper has been read.

62 63
64 Gray, R. Two Approaches and Comparative Training Studies infographics, perceptionaction.com. Local copies: two-approaches.md (last row) and comparative-training-studies.md (study 17, Caldeira et al. 2023, volleyball). The comparative table is the page to bring when someone pushes back. 65
66 67
68 This course’s extension, not the paper’s 69

In return to performance the reflex regression is to strip the drill to no opponent. On the logic above that does not simplify the task. It deletes it, and it deletes exactly the perception the returning athlete has to rebuild. Parry et al. write about skill development, not rehabilitation. Applying it to return to performance is our step, and you should say so when you cite it.

70
71 72

4. What the paper does not say

73 74

It does not say “never unopposed.” Read it fairly, because the first physician who has read it will.

75 76
    77
  • Unopposed work has a place as exploration: a chance to search many ways of moving with little consequence, not to perfect one technique by repetition (pp. 3–6).
    • 78
  • Unopposed drills can be made alive by putting other moving bodies in the same space, even when nobody is defending anyone (pp. 4–5).
    • 79
  • There is “limited evidence to suggest that unopposed practice must precede opposed, game-like practice” (p. 6). The ladder you were taught is a habit, not a finding.
    • 80
81 82

So the claim you can defend is narrower and stronger than “opposed is better.” It is this: an unopposed drill is not evidence of readiness, because the information the athlete times up is the information that is missing. Use unopposed work to build capacity and to explore. Do not use it to prove anything.

83 84
85
86
87 No opponentBodies in the spaceOpponent, pressure downLive opponent 88
89
90

Readiness lives on the right half of that bar. Regress along it. Do not jump off it.
